subtitle: Recognize work that classification and pay decisions can miss, document duties accurately, and bring classification and pay questions to Human Resources and labor relations with the facts they need.
audience: For DHS and DSD supervisors, managers, program and policy leads, and staff who write position descriptions, assign work or raise questions about how work is classified and paid. It builds on the supervisor course on who carries equity work.

lessons.title: Work the classification does not name
objectives: Explain how a classification system values work through recorded duties, using the factors Minnesota law names.
Identify four kinds of work that often go unrecorded: interpreting, cultural brokering, informal training of others and emotional labor.
Distinguish noticing a pattern of unrecorded work from predicting who does it based on identity.
Describe the costs of unrecorded work to the employee, the team and the people served.
lessons.teaching:
In Minnesota's executive branch, a class is one or more positions similar enough in duties and responsibilities that the same title and pay schedule can apply to them equitably. That definition, in Minnesota Statutes section 43A.02, explains why recorded duties matter so much. The same section defines the comparability of the value of the work as the composite of the skill, effort, responsibility and working conditions the work normally requires. A classification system can only weigh what it can see. Duties that never appear in a position description, a work plan or an assignment record have no way to count when a position is allocated to a class or when the value of a class is compared with others.

Four kinds of work go unrecorded often enough to name. Interpreting happens when a bilingual employee is asked to explain a notice, return a family's call or sit in on a meeting because they speak the language. Cultural brokering goes further: the employee explains what a process means to a family, why a community might hesitate, or how a message is likely to be heard, and colleagues come to rely on that judgment. Informal training of others shows up when an experienced worker becomes the person everyone asks, walks new staff through systems and reviews drafts, though no one assigned it. Emotional labor is the work of managing feelings, one's own and other people's, as part of the job: steadying a distressed caller, absorbing a provider's frustration, or keeping a tense meeting productive. Each takes skill and effort, and some carry real responsibility for outcomes.

These tasks tend to go unrecorded for ordinary reasons. They arrive a few minutes at a time, they feel like helping rather than working, and they are often treated as part of who someone is rather than what they do. A supervisor may be glad the work gets done and reluctant to look closely at what it costs. Over time the person doing it carries a fuller job than the classification describes, and their assigned work may slip in ways that show up in their review. The program comes to depend on a skill it has never acknowledged and could lose without warning. People served may also receive help, such as an untrained interpretation of a notice, that no one has checked for accuracy.

There is a careful line here. A pattern of unrecorded work is worth examining, and in many workplaces it follows language, culture, disability or long tenure. It is not a reason to assume that a particular employee does this work, wants it or should be given it because of who they are. Start with the work itself: what was done, how often, for whom and with what effect. That keeps the question on duties, which is where classification and pay decisions are made, and away from identity, which should never drive an assignment. Whether a staff member may interpret for members of the public at all, and with what qualifications, is a separate language access question for the person or area responsible.
lessons.keyPoint: A classification system can only value the duties it can see. Start with the work that was done, how often and for whom, not with who you expect to have done it.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{SUPERVISOR}} is updating work plans and notices that {{CASE_MANAGER}} spends part of most weeks returning calls from families who speak a language {{CASE_MANAGER}} also speaks, explaining program letters and advising colleagues on how to approach those families. None of this appears in the position description. {{CASE_MANAGER}} has said the work matters to them and also that their own case notes are falling behind.
lessons.question: What is the strongest first step for {{SUPERVISOR}}?
choices: Thank {{CASE_MANAGER}} at the next team meeting so the extra work gets the recognition it has been missing.
Route every family who speaks that language to {{CASE_MANAGER}} so the work shows up in caseload counts.
Ask {{CASE_MANAGER}} to help list the tasks, how often they happen and what they accomplish.
feedback: Recognition matters, and it may be welcome. It does not change what the position description says or what the classification can see, and public thanks can mark someone as the go-to person for even more of the same work.

This assigns work by language without asking whether that design is right, whether interpreting by staff meets language access expectations, or whether {{CASE_MANAGER}} wants it. It also adds to a load that is already slipping.

This starts with the work rather than identity, gives {{CASE_MANAGER}} a voice in how it is described, and produces the record any later conversation with Human Resources will need. It also brings tasks such as interpreting into view as a language access question.
lessons.reflection: Privately think of a task in your unit that someone does regularly but that appears nowhere in writing, or use the practice case. What skill does it take, and what would happen to the work and the people served if that person left tomorrow?
lessons.action: For two weeks, keep a simple log of unassigned work you ask for or see on your team: the task, roughly how long it took and who benefited. Describe tasks, not anyone's background or identity, and use the log to decide which duties belong in writing.

check.question: Under Minnesota Statutes section 43A.02, which factors make up the comparability of the value of the work?
check.correct: The skill, effort, responsibility and working conditions the work normally requires.
wrong: Seniority, education and the employee's most recent performance rating.
Job title, pay grade and the number of people the position supervises.
check.feedback: The statute measures value by the composite of skill, effort, responsibility and working conditions the work normally requires. That is why unrecorded duties matter: a factor can only be weighed when the work behind it is documented.

lessons.title: Documenting duties so the record matches the work
objectives: Explain what a position description is used for, as Minnesota Management and Budget describes it.
Write duty statements that describe the work, its frequency and its responsibility without inflating or shrinking it.
Distinguish occasional help from regular duties and decide what belongs in writing.
Weigh the trade-offs of formalizing work, including workload, service quality and the employee's choice.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota Management and Budget describes an accurate position description as an HR requirement, used primarily for classification and for filling vacancies, and also as a practical tool for everyday supervision and performance coaching. Its guidance suggests identifying five to seven principal responsibilities and cautions that a description much longer than four pages is unlikely to work as a management tool. These uses pull in the same direction. A description that matches the work tells the employee what is expected, helps a supervisor coach, and gives Human Resources an accurate picture when a classification question comes up.

Accuracy cuts both ways. Leaving out regular interpreting or training understates the job. Writing every helpful moment into the description, or using stronger verbs than the work supports, overstates it, and an overstated description can create its own problems when Human Resources reviews it or when the position is next filled. Good duty statements say what is done, for whom, how often and with what responsibility. "Explains program notices by phone to families in a second language several times a week and flags concerns to the assigned worker" is more useful than "provides cultural expertise." The first describes work that someone can evaluate; the second describes a trait. Duty statements should also be broad enough that ordinary changes in the work still fit within them.

The harder judgment is what belongs in writing at all. Occasional help is part of working on a team. Regular, expected work that takes real time is a duty, whether or not anyone assigned it. When a task has become a duty, a supervisor has several honest choices: write it into the description and make room by moving other work; share or rotate it so it does not settle on one person; obtain the service another way, such as through qualified interpreters or a defined training role; or stop asking for it. Each choice has costs. Formalizing interpreting may place an employee in a role they did not choose and may raise qualification questions. Moving the work elsewhere may lose relationships that families value. The employee's view belongs in this decision, and so does the program's obligation to the people it serves.

Documenting duties also has limits. A supervisor can describe the work accurately and talk it through with the employee, but formal employment decisions, including how a position is classified and paid, stay with Human Resources and, for classification, with Minnesota Management and Budget under state law. The rules that apply can also depend on the collective bargaining agreement or compensation plan that covers the position. Contracts and plans differ, so ask before you describe any expected outcome to an employee. Keep the record about duties. Do not write an employee's background, health, language identity or personal circumstances into a description; write the skill the work requires.
lessons.keyPoint: Describe the work, how often it happens and what responsibility it carries. An accurate record neither shrinks nor inflates the job, and it gives Human Resources what it needs for any classification question.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} is revising position descriptions for a unit after a reorganization. {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} points out that one experienced worker has trained every new hire for three years, reviews drafts for the team and is the first call for system questions, and suggests writing "serves as team lead" into that worker's description so the work is finally recognized.
lessons.question: How should {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} respond to the suggestion?
choices: Write the training and support duties with their frequency, review them with the worker, then ask HR.
Use the lead title, since it is the clearest way to show the worker's contribution has grown past the job.
Leave the description unchanged until the worker formally asks Human Resources for a classification review.
feedback: This records the work in terms Human Resources can evaluate, gives the worker a say in how it is described, and leaves the classification question with the people who decide it.

The intent is good, but a title can imply responsibilities, such as directing others' work, that this work may not include. An overstated record can backfire when it is reviewed or when the position is filled again.
Waiting puts the whole burden on the worker and leaves the record inaccurate in the meantime. A supervisor can describe the duties correctly without deciding anything about classification.
lessons.reflection: Privately compare a position description you know well, perhaps your own, with what the work involves now. Which duties are missing, and which are written more strongly or more weakly than the work supports?
lessons.action: Choose one position description you are responsible for. Rewrite one duty so it says what is done, for whom, how often and with what responsibility. Review the change with the employee before it goes to Human Resources.

check.question: According to Minnesota Management and Budget, what is a position description used for primarily?
check.correct: Classification and filling vacancies, with everyday supervision as another important use.
wrong: Setting each employee's salary within the pay range for the class.
Recording the employee's performance rating for the review period.
check.feedback: MMB describes the position description as an HR requirement used primarily for classification and vacancy filling, and also as a practical tool for supervision and coaching. Salary placement and performance ratings follow other rules and processes.

lessons.title: Work out of class, classification reviews and their trade-offs
objectives: Explain when Administrative Procedure 17.1 on work out of class applies and when it does not.
Describe the routes in Minnesota Statutes section 43A.07 for investigating and protesting a position's classification.
Weigh the possible risks and benefits of a classification review for the person in the position.
Prepare a factual request to Human Resources and labor relations without promising an outcome.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota Management and Budget Administrative Procedure 17.1, last revised January 29, 2024, covers work out of class. It applies when an agency temporarily assigns a permanent or probationary classified employee to perform substantially all the duties of a temporarily unoccupied classified position in a different classification within the agency. The employee is not appointed to the other class. The procedure does not apply when someone temporarily takes on some supervisory duties, or some but not substantially all of another position's duties. The contract or plan that covers the employee's permanent class controls eligibility, the minimum time before any differential is paid, the differential itself and related pay questions, and the procedure says to review it first. Assignments generally may not exceed one year without an exception under the contract or plan or approval from Minnesota Management and Budget, and agency HR must get approval from MMB Labor Relations before extending an assignment to a probationary employee.

Much unrecognized work does not fit that procedure. Interpreting, cultural brokering and informal training usually happen alongside a person's own job, not in place of an unoccupied position. When duties have changed in lasting ways, the question is classification instead. Minnesota Statutes section 43A.07 gives the commissioner of Minnesota Management and Budget responsibility for the classification plan. The commissioner may investigate the duties of a classified position at the request of a permanent employee, and if that request is denied, the employee receives a written explanation. The commissioner must investigate at the request of an appointing authority. An affected appointing authority may protest an allocation or reclassification, and an affected employee may protest a reclassification, in writing to the commissioner. Ask Human Resources how these steps work in practice at DHS, and do not describe a process to an employee that you have not confirmed.

A classification review is not automatically a gain for the employee. Section 43A.07 also says that when a position is reclassified, the incumbent continues in it only if eligible for and appointed to the new class, and that otherwise, unless the employee is transferred, promoted or demoted, the layoff provisions of the applicable plan or collective bargaining agreement apply. A review may also conclude that the work fits the current class, or that some duties belong in another position. These are reasons to involve Human Resources and labor relations early and to help the employee make an informed choice. They are not reasons to avoid the question. Never present a review as a raise, and never discourage someone from asking for one.

A useful request is factual. It describes the duties as they are, when they began, how often they are performed, what responsibility they carry and what changed. It does not argue from identity or financial need, and it does not rest on a supervisor's view of what the employee deserves. While a question is pending, a supervisor can still act within their own authority: adjust workload, stop relying on unassigned work, or arrange the service another way. Represented employees may choose to talk with their union, and that choice is theirs. Ask Human Resources and labor relations what the contract or plan says about differentials, timing and retroactive pay rather than guessing.
lessons.keyPoint: Work out of class and a classification review answer different questions, and each follows rules set by procedure, statute and the applicable contract or plan. Bring dated facts, involve HR and labor relations early, and never promise an outcome.
lessons.example: Practice case: For eight months {{CASE_MANAGER}} has trained new staff, reviewed complex files and covered some tasks of a vacant lead position, while keeping a full caseload. {{CASE_MANAGER}} asks {{SUPERVISOR}} whether this counts as work out of class and whether {{SUPERVISOR}} can get the extra pay approved.
lessons.question: What should {{SUPERVISOR}} say?
choices: Yes, this is clearly work out of class, so you should receive the differential for all the months already worked.
Let's document the duties and dates and ask HR and labor relations, because the answer depends on the rules.
Probably not, since you kept your own caseload, so there is likely nothing to request or raise with anyone.
feedback: Covering some tasks of a vacant position may not meet the procedure's test of substantially all the duties, and any pay depends on the contract or plan. A promise the supervisor cannot keep damages trust.

This takes the question seriously without deciding it. A dated record of duties is what Human Resources and labor relations need to tell whether work out of class, a classification question or a workload change is the right response.
This may be partly right about the procedure, but it closes the door on a classification or workload question that deserves a look. Discouraging a request is not a supervisor's call to make.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider whether anyone on your team has been covering part of another role for months. What would they need to know before deciding whether to ask for a review, and who could tell them?
lessons.action: Find the work out of class provisions in the contract or plan that covers your team, and write down two questions about them for Human Resources or labor relations before you need the answers.

check.question: When does Administrative Procedure 17.1 on work out of class apply?
check.correct: When an eligible employee temporarily performs substantially all the duties of an unoccupied position in another class.
wrong: Whenever an employee takes on any duty that is not in their position description.
Once an employee has performed extra duties of any kind for at least one year.
check.feedback: The procedure covers substantially all the duties of a temporarily unoccupied classified position in a different class. Taking on some duties, or some supervisory duties, does not meet that test, though it may still raise a classification or workload question.

lessons.title: Minnesota's pay equity history and what it does not settle
objectives: Describe the 1982 state law on equitable compensation relationships and the policy now in Minnesota Statutes section 43A.01.
Explain how state law defines female-dominated, male-dominated and balanced classes and how compensation inequities are reported.
Identify what a class-based pay equity policy can and cannot address, including undervalued duties and patterns by race, language or disability.
Route each kind of pay concern to the person or area responsible with evidence about duties and classes.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota addressed pay equity for its own executive branch employees in 1982. Laws 1982, chapter 634, approved March 23, 1982, provided for equitable compensation relationships among certain government employees. Its policy appears today in Minnesota Statutes section 43A.01, subdivision 3: the state attempts to establish equitable compensation relationships between female-dominated, male-dominated and balanced classes of executive branch employees, and those relationships are equitable when the primary consideration in setting total compensation is the comparability of the value of the work in relation to other executive branch positions. The 1982 law also changed the factors used to compare positions to the four still in statute: skill, effort, responsibility and working conditions.

The definitions show how the policy works. Under section 43A.02, a female-dominated class is one in which more than 70 percent of incumbents are female, a male-dominated class is one in which more than 80 percent are male, and a balanced class has no more than 80 percent male and no more than 70 percent female incumbents. Section 43A.05, subdivision 5, still directs the commissioner of Minnesota Management and Budget to submit, by January 1 of each odd-numbered year, a list of female-dominated and male-dominated classes for which a compensation inequity exists based on the comparability of the value of the work, with an estimated cost. The policy compares classes, not individuals, and its results depend on how the work of each class has been valued.

That design connects directly to the work in this course. A class-based policy can only correct what job evaluation sees. If interpreting, cultural brokering, informal training or emotional labor are missing from position descriptions and class specifications, they may be missing from the value assigned to the class as well. As written in chapter 43A, the pay equity policy is framed around the sex composition of classes; it does not by its terms address patterns by race, national origin, language or disability, which other laws and processes may reach. It also does not settle whether one person is paid fairly, which depends on classification, the contract or plan and individual pay decisions. Treat the history as evidence that the state chose to examine how work is valued, and as a reminder that valuing work depends on recording it.

Pay concerns can arise at several levels: one person's pay, a position's classification, the way a class is valued, or a possible pattern of discrimination. Each goes somewhere different. Questions about individual pay and classification go to Human Resources, and to labor relations where a contract is involved. Questions about how classes are valued sit with Minnesota Management and Budget. A concern that pay or assignments differ because of race, sex, disability or another protected trait is a possible discrimination concern and goes promptly to the person or area responsible, such as the Equal Opportunity and Access Division or Human Resources, without waiting for a pattern to be proven. Your contribution at every level is the same: an accurate record of duties and a clear account of what you have observed.
lessons.keyPoint: Minnesota's pay equity policy compares the value of work across classes using skill, effort, responsibility and working conditions. It can only value what is recorded, and it does not settle every pay concern, so route each concern to the person or area responsible.
lessons.example: Practice case: During a team discussion, {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}} says that Minnesota solved pay equity for state workers in the 1980s, so any pay concern now must be about individual performance. {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} knows several staff carry interpreting and training work that is not in their descriptions and wants to respond accurately.
lessons.question: What is the most accurate response for {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}}?
choices: Agree that the 1982 law settled pay equity, and suggest that anyone with a pay concern raise it at their performance review.
Say the 1982 law has little to do with today's work, since it applied only to the jobs that existed back then.
Explain that the policy compares how classes are valued, which relies on recorded duties, and other concerns go elsewhere.
feedback: The policy remains in statute with ongoing reporting, and it compares classes rather than individuals. A performance review is not the route for a classification or pay concern.
The policy is current law, not a one-time event, and section 43A.05 still calls for a list every odd-numbered year. Dismissing it misses why recording duties matters now.
This is accurate about what the policy does and does not do, connects it to the unrecorded work on the team, and points people toward the right routes without deciding their concerns.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider a kind of job you know that is held mostly by people of one gender. Which duties in that work might be easy to overlook in a job evaluation, and how would you know?
lessons.action: Pick one class specification that covers positions on your team and compare its listed duties with the work your team actually does. Note any regular duties that are missing, and share the note with Human Resources as a question, not a conclusion.

check.question: Under Minnesota Statutes section 43A.02, what makes a class female-dominated?
check.correct: More than 70 percent of its incumbents are female.
wrong: More than 50 percent of its incumbents are female.
More than 80 percent of its incumbents are female.
check.feedback: State law uses different thresholds: more than 70 percent female for a female-dominated class and more than 80 percent male for a male-dominated class. A balanced class has no more than 80 percent male and no more than 70 percent female incumbents.

cards.back: One or more positions similar enough in duties and responsibilities that the same title and pay schedule can apply to them equitably (Minnesota Statutes section 43A.02).

cards.front: Comparability of the value of the work
cards.back: The composite of the skill, effort, responsibility and working conditions the work normally requires. Only recorded duties can be weighed.
Regular, expected work, such as interpreting, cultural brokering, informal training of others or emotional labor, that appears in no position description or assignment record.
What is done, for whom, how often and with what responsibility. It describes work that can be evaluated, not a personal trait.
Temporarily performing substantially all the duties of an unoccupied classified position in a different class (MMB Administrative Procedure 17.1). Eligibility and pay depend on the contract or plan.

Under section 43A.07, MMB may investigate a classified position's duties at a permanent employee's request, with a written explanation if it declines, and must investigate at an appointing authority's request.
The state policy since 1982 that pay across female-dominated, male-dominated and balanced executive branch classes rests primarily on the comparability of the value of the work.

aid.heading: See the work
items: Log unassigned tasks for two weeks: the task, the time and who benefited.
Look for interpreting, cultural brokering, informal training and emotional labor.
Start from the work, never from assumptions about who does it.
Treat staff interpreting for the public as a language access question.

aid.heading: Document duties
items: Write what is done, for whom, how often and with what responsibility.
Neither shrink nor inflate the job; avoid titles the work does not support.
Decide whether to formalize, share, obtain the work another way or stop asking for it.
Leave background, health and identity out; name the skill the work requires.

aid.heading: Route the question
items: Substantially all of a vacant position's duties: ask HR about work out of class.
Lasting change in duties: ask HR about a classification investigation.
Check the contract or plan first; contracts and plans differ.
Possible discrimination in pay or assignments: report promptly to the person or area responsible.

aid.heading: Talk with the employee
items: Explain what you know and who decides.
Never promise a raise and never discourage a request.
Point out that reclassification can have consequences for the incumbent, and have HR explain them.
Respect that represented employees may choose to talk with their union.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 43A.01 — Policies
sources.note: Subdivision 3 states the policy on equitable compensation relationships between female-dominated, male-dominated and balanced executive branch classes; the history line lists 1982 chapter 634 (lesson 4). Read November 25, 2026, in the 2025 statutes.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 43A.02 — Definitions
sources.note: Defines class, position, comparability of the value of the work, and female-dominated, male-dominated and balanced classes with their percentage thresholds (lessons 1 and 4). Does not define a classification plan.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 43A.05 — Powers and responsibilities; personnel
sources.note: Subdivision 1 gives the commissioner responsibility for the classification plan and compensation plans; subdivision 5 requires the odd-year list of classes with compensation inequities (lesson 4). The course does not report what any recent list contained.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 43A.07 — Classified service
sources.note: Supports the routes for investigating and protesting allocation and reclassification, the written explanation when an employee's request is denied, and the effect of reclassification on the incumbent (lesson 3). How DHS handles these steps in practice was not reviewed; ask Human Resources.

sources.title: Laws of Minnesota 1982, chapter 634 — Equitable compensation relationships
sources.note: Session law approved March 23, 1982, that set the policy, definitions and reporting for state executive branch classes and changed the comparison factors to skill, effort, responsibility and working conditions (lesson 4). Historical text; the current statutes govern.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Administrative Procedure 17.1, Work Out of Class Assignments (revised 2024)
sources.note: Supports the definition, exclusions, role of the contract or plan, one-year limit and approvals for work out of class (lesson 3). Last revised January 29, 2024; check for later revisions.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Position Descriptions
sources.note: Supports the statement that position descriptions are an HR requirement used primarily for classification and vacancy filling and also support supervision, and the guidance on principal responsibilities and length (lesson 2). It does not describe a reclassification process.
